edges.description: Aggregates disrupt the periodic submembranous lattice at the axon initial segment.
Inhibitory innervation falls when alpha-II spectrin function is lost, by a route that has not been mapped.
Neuronal process development is altered in the same systems.
Loss of sodium-channel clustering at the initial segment raises the threshold for firing in the affected neuron.
Fewer inhibitory inputs leave cortical networks disinhibited.
Abnormal process development plausibly contributes to the lamination defect seen on loss of alpha-II spectrin.
A disinhibited immature cortex generates the presenting epilepsy.
Shows the defining aggregation phenotype in human neurons at the patient genotype, which neither the null mouse nor the R1098Q mouse can do.
edges.limitations: iPSC neurons are developmentally immature and lack the circuit context in which the epilepsy arises, so they establish the cell-biological lesion rather than the network phenotype. The developmental defects were characterised alongside overexpression experiments in rodent neurons, so the patient-derived arm of that comparison is the smaller part of the evidence.

edges.description: Establishes that alpha-II spectrin is required for axon initial segment assembly, which is the structural premise the human aggregation mechanism acts on.
edges.limitations: A complete deletion removes the protein rather than producing an aggregating mutant, so it shows what the AIS needs alpha-II spectrin for, not how the human variant disrupts it. The mice die before one month, far short of the human disease course.

edges.description: Reproduces the cortical developmental defect, and pairs it with seizures and neurodegeneration in the same animals.
edges.limitations: Same null-versus-dominant-negative caveat; and because the deletion is CNS-wide from development, the model cannot separate a cell-autonomous lamination defect from a consequence of widespread degeneration.

edges.description: A null cannot aggregate. This model deletes the protein, so it cannot reproduce the dominant-negative sequestration that defines the human mechanism, and any phenotype it shows is evidence about requirement rather than about aggregation.
edges.limitations: This is a definitional limitation rather than an experimental shortfall, and it is the reason the entry does not treat the conditional knockout as a model of DEE5 as such. The point is sharpened by the observation that heterozygous null mice - the closest null analogue of a heterozygous human patient - have no phenotype at all, so gene dose alone does not reproduce the disease.

edges.description: Heterozygous R1098Q mice have seizure episodes, so a dominant-negative alpha-II spectrin allele is sufficient to produce seizures in vivo. The seizures are stress-induced and appear alongside progressive ataxia and memory impairment.
edges.limitations: The variant is in repeat 10, not the heterodimerization repeats that cause DEE5, and the phenotype it produces - progressive ataxia with stress-induced seizures and memory impairment - resembles the milder ataxia end of the human SPTAN1 spectrum more than infantile spasms with hypsarrhythmia. It therefore supports the dominant-negative principle without modelling this disease's epilepsy syndrome.

nodes.description: Alpha-II spectrin partners with beta-IV spectrin to form the periodic cytoskeleton of the axon initial segment. Aggregation disrupts that lattice and, with it, the clustering of ankyrin-G and voltage-gated sodium channels that depends on it.

nodes.description: Neurons derived from patients carrying dominant-negative SPTAN1 variants - the one system that carries the actual human genotype rather than a null or a surrogate allele.

An in-frame deletion or duplication in the last two spectrin repeats of the C-terminal region, the site at which alpha/beta spectrin heterodimer nucleation begins. Position and variant type are both load-bearing here: only in-frame changes in this region produce the severe phenotype, which is why this node names the region rather than simply recording "a SPTAN1 variant".

nodes.description: Neurons bearing spectrin aggregates fire less readily, not more. This node is curated in the direction the measurement actually went, which is opposite to what an epilepsy entry would naively predict; the discussion attached to it addresses how a disorder of reduced single-neuron excitability produces seizures.

nodes.description: Inhibitory innervation decreases after alpha-II spectrin loss. This is the arm that plausibly reconciles the seizures with the elevated single-neuron threshold above, by removing inhibition at network level rather than by making individual neurons more excitable.

nodes.description: A spontaneous point mutation affecting alpha-II spectrin scaffold stability, and the closest available in vivo analogue of a human dominant-negative allele - though it sits in repeat 10 rather than the last two repeats that cause DEE5.

Complete CNS deletion of alpha-II spectrin. Supplies the structural and developmental arms of this entry. Note the deliberate mismatch of mechanism: this is a null, whereas human DEE5 is dominant-negative, which is why its relationship to the aggregation node is typed as a failure to recapitulate.

Mutant and wild-type alpha-II spectrin both assemble heterodimers with beta-II spectrin, but the mutant heterodimers are thermolabile. This is a distinct node from the aggregation it leads to, and the distinction matters: assembly is not blocked, so the defect is in the stability of a complex that does form, not in failure to form one.
